“stooped to truth and moralized his song”﻿ Spring pricks a little. I get out the maps. Time to demoralize my song, high time. Vernal a little. Primavera. First Green, first truth and last. High time, high time. A high old time we had of it last summer? I overstate. But getting out the maps… Look! Up the valley of the Brenne, Louise de la Vallière… Syntax collapses. High time for that, high time. To Château-Renault, the tannery town whose marquis Rooke and James Butler whipped in Vigo Bay Or so the song says, an amoral song Like Ronsard’s where we go today Perhaps, perhaps tomorrow. Tomorrow and tomorrow and… Get well! Philip’s black-sailed familiar, avaunt Or some word as ridiculous, the whole Diction kit begins to fall apart. High time it did, high time. High time and a long time yet, my love! Get out that blessed map. Ageing, you take your glasses off to read it. Stooping to truth, we potter to Montoire. High time, my love. High time and a long time yet.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Spring, Time, Vernal

outputs.L1:
“Stooped to truth and moralized his song.”

Spring pricks a little. I get out the maps. It is time to demoralize my song—high time. Vernal, a little. Primavera. First green, first truth, and last. High time, high time.

A high old time we had of it last summer? I overstate. But getting out the maps—look! Up the valley of the Brenne: Louise de la Vallière…

Syntax collapses. High time for that; high time.

To Château-Renault, the tannery town, whose Marquis Rooke and James Butler whipped in Vigo Bay—or so the song says: an amoral song, like Ronsard’s, where we go today, perhaps; perhaps tomorrow. Tomorrow and tomorrow and…

Get well! Philip’s black-sailed familiar, avaunt—or some word as ridiculous. The whole diction kit begins to fall apart. High time it did; high time.

High time, and a long time yet, my love! Get out that blessed map. Ageing, you take your glasses off to read it. Stooping to truth, we potter to Montoire.

High time, my love. High time, and a long time yet.
outputs.L2:
“bent down toward fact and turned his music into a lesson”

Spring has a faint sting to it. I unfold the maps. It is time—past time—to strip the moral weight from my song. A touch of springtime: vernal, primavera. The first green appears, the first truth, and the final one. It is late already, very late. Did we have some grand, glorious time last summer? No, I exaggerate. Still, once the maps are spread out…

See there: up the Brenne valley, toward Louise de la Vallière… The grammar gives way. It is time for that too, long past time. On to Château-Renault, the town of tanneries, whose marquis, so the song claims, was beaten by Rooke and James Butler in Vigo Bay. Or so that amoral song has it, a song like Ronsard’s, the kind we may follow today—perhaps today, perhaps tomorrow. Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and…

Recover! Away with Philip’s black-sailed attendant—begone, or whatever absurd word will do. The whole apparatus of elevated language starts coming apart. And rightly so: it is time, well past time. Yet there is still a long while to go, my love. Bring out that blessed map. Growing older, you remove your glasses in order to read it. Lowering ourselves toward the truth, we wander on to Montoire. It is time, my love. High time—and still a long time yet.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents spring as a season of renewal, but it does not treat renewal as simple or innocent. The speaker welcomes the return of life, movement, and freshness, yet this seasonal beginning also becomes an occasion for questioning inherited ways of thinking. Old assumptions about truth, morality, and poetic expression no longer seem secure. Spring does not merely restore the world; it unsettles it. The speaker seems to ask whether the familiar habits of language and judgment are still adequate to describe experience.

The image of getting out maps suggests travel in a literal sense, as though the speaker and a companion might set off across landscapes and revisit particular places. However, the maps also point toward a more inward journey. They chart memory, history, and language as much as geography. To unfold a map is to confront the past, to trace routes already taken, and to imagine possible futures. In this way, movement through space becomes a form of reflection: the speaker travels through personal memory, cultural reference, and the accumulated meanings of words.

Throughout the poem, references to places, historical figures, and literary echoes create a deliberately shifting and fragmented texture. These allusions do not settle into a single, stable argument. Instead, they produce a meditation on time and meaning that feels restless and associative. The poem moves between the personal and the historical, between immediate feeling and inherited culture. Its fragments suggest that experience itself is broken, layered, and difficult to organize into a clear pattern.

This sense of disorder is reinforced by the poem’s repeated insistence that it is “high time” for language itself to change. Syntax, diction, and poetic convention seem ready to break down or be remade. The poem challenges the idea that traditional forms can still fully express modern consciousness. Its play with language becomes more than stylistic experiment; it is a way of dramatizing the need for renewal. Just as spring remakes the natural world, poetry must remake its own means of expression.

Yet beneath the poem’s playful disorder and intellectual restlessness, there is a deeply human tenderness. The speaker addresses a beloved companion with affection and desire, even while acknowledging aging, uncertainty, and the passage of time. The poem’s disruptions do not erase intimacy; rather, they make it more poignant. In a world where meanings shift and certainties collapse, the continuing presence of the beloved becomes a source of warmth and connection. The poem therefore balances experiment with emotion, presenting renewal not only as a linguistic or artistic necessity but also as a personal act of love and endurance.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a fragmented meditation on aging, memory, love, and the uncertain nature of poetic truth. Rather than developing a single argument in a linear way, it moves associatively through images of springtime renewal, maps, literary echoes, and moments of syntactic breakdown. This shifting structure reflects the speaker’s own sense of instability: the world can still appear fresh and vivid, yet the mind that receives it is marked by time, loss, and accumulated memory.

Spring is important because it traditionally suggests rebirth, energy, and new beginnings. In the poem, however, renewal is not simple or innocent. The season arrives alongside an awareness of age, as if new life can only be perceived through the knowledge that youth has passed. This tension gives the poem much of its emotional force. The speaker recognizes beauty, but that beauty is shadowed by the awareness that perception itself is changing. Memory does not preserve the past perfectly; instead, it fragments and rearranges it, making the past feel both intimate and unreachable.

The references to maps suggest a desire for orientation. A map promises clarity, distance, and control: it organizes space into legible forms. Yet the poem questions whether such forms can truly contain lived experience. Place is not merely geographical; it is emotional, historical, and relational. The speaker’s movement through mapped or remembered landscapes becomes a way of asking how one locates oneself in time, in language, and in relation to another person. The poem’s literary allusions deepen this uncertainty, placing the speaker’s private reflections within a wider tradition while also revealing the limits of inherited language. Poetry offers patterns and precedents, but it cannot fully stabilize experience.

As the poem progresses, its syntax begins to loosen or collapse. This formal instability mirrors the weakening of certainty. Words no longer seem able to claim authority in the way they once might have. Diction, like youth, falls away; polished expression gives way to hesitation, interruption, and humility. Yet this loss is not presented simply as failure. Instead, the poem suggests that truth may become more accessible when language stops pretending to master reality. To “stoop to truth” is to lower oneself from abstraction, pride, or rhetorical grandeur toward something more modest and immediate.

The poem’s central insight is that even when certainty, eloquence, and youth diminish, shared attention remains meaningful. Love survives not as a grand ideal but as a practice of noticing: looking together at a place, remembering together, and accepting the partial nature of what can be known or said. In this sense, the act of stooping to truth is both humble and sustaining. It acknowledges human limitation while preserving the possibility of connection. The poem ultimately finds value not in perfect knowledge or permanent renewal, but in the fragile, attentive love that continues amid change.
outputs.L5:
Spring is a season of renewal, a time when the world slowly awakens from winter’s quiet rest. As the days grow longer and the air becomes warmer, nature begins to bloom with fresh color and life. Trees open their buds, flowers rise from the soil, and birds return with songs that fill the morning.

This vernal season reminds us of growth, hope, and new beginnings. The word “vernal” is often used to describe the beauty and freshness of spring, especially the gentle changes that come with the season. It is a time to enjoy sunlight, breathe in the scent of blossoms, and appreciate the simple joy of watching the earth come alive again.

Spring teaches us that change can be beautiful. After the cold and darkness of winter, the vernal warmth returns, bringing energy, light, and promise. It is a perfect time to start something new, spend more moments outdoors, and welcome the peaceful rhythm of nature.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem that begins with the line “stooped to truth and moralized his song,” then twists it into “demoralize my song,” mixing springtime, maps, French place names, aging love, and literary allusions to Shakespeare, Ronsard, and “Get well, Philip.”
counterfactuals.output:
stooped to truth and moralized his song,  
someone said of Shakespeare, maybe,  
as if the heart were a courtroom  
and spring only evidence  
pinned to the corkboard:  
forsythia, rain, a bruise of violets  
under the park bench.

But I am older now,  
and love has learned to read the legend  
before trusting the map.  
Here is Paris, here is Tours,  
here the Loire loosening its silver sentence  
past Amboise and Blois,  
past all the châteaux  
where desire once put on a collar  
and called itself eternity.

Ronsard, with his roses,  
keeps leaning from the margin—  
cueillez, cueillez—  
as if time were a flower stall  
and not a pharmacist  
counting out the little white moons  
of another morning.

My darling, we have crossed  
so many folded countries together  
the creases have become roads:  
Avignon in the wrist,  
Marseille in the throat,  
Chartres lit blue behind the ribs.  
Even our arguments have suburbs now,  
with bakeries, roundabouts,  
a municipal fountain no one visits.

Spring comes anyway,  
vulgar and forgiving,  
green pushing through the grammar  
of last year’s leaves.  
The young kiss in doorways  
with the insolence of weather.  
We walk past them slowly,  
two annotated editions  
of a play nobody finishes.

Get well, Philip,  
someone writes on a card,  
and literature coughs in the next room,  
turning its face toward the wall.  
The sonnets keep their fever.  
The roses rot beautifully.  
The map refolds itself  
along the old imperial lines.

So let the moralists have their music,  
their tidy endings,  
their tragic kings arranged like cutlery.  
I want the detour,  
the torn corner,  
the town whose name I mispronounce  
and love more for it.

I want to demoralize my song—  
take virtue out of its stiff black coat,  
let it wander hatless through the rain,  
let it buy cherries in Orléans,  
let it forget the lesson  
and remember the mouth.

Because you are still here,  
because I am still here,  
because April keeps making a scandal  
of the trees,  
I will not conclude.  
I will only unfold the map again  
between us,

and where the river bends,  
where the ink has thinned  
from years of touching,  
I will place my finger  
and say:  
this is where we are.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, allusive poem in the style of late modernist British poetry, about an older couple looking at maps in spring and planning a trip through the Loire region, with references to Louise de la Vallière, Château-Renault, Vigo Bay, and the phrase “High time.”
counterfactuals.output:
**High Time**

Spring unrolls her green-inked sheets; the table  
blooms with départements, rivers, little wounds  
of roads stippled east to west. Your hand, still steady,  
pins Tours beneath a cup-ring moon. Mine wanders  
towards Château-Renault, where the name clinks  
like bridles in a vanished yard, like rain  
on roofs of slate and tanneries’ dark water.

“High time,” you say—not sadly, not quite glad—  
and fold the phrase into the map’s old creases,  
as though it were a pass, a lettre de cachet,  
or some last dispensation from the spring.  
Outside, the pear-tree whitens; bees rehearse  
their small gold engines. We, who have outlived  
three radiators, two empires of desire,  
and most of what we meant by “afterwards,”  
plot Blois, Amboise, Chenonceau: pale chessmen  
set beside the Loire’s long, lucid argument.

Louise de la Vallière flickers in the margin—  
the limp, the veil, the king’s sun at her shoulder,  
love’s lacquer cracked to convent ash. We pause  
where history, that draught beneath the door,  
touches our ankles. You laugh: “Not Versailles, then?”  
No. Let us have the lesser road, the inn  
with nettles at the stair, the wine that tastes  
of flint and weather, and the evening bell  
counting no victories.

Yet Vigo Bay returns—  
why, after all these years?—a cold blue pocket  
on another chart: lost bullion, sunk ambition,  
the wrecks gone green beneath Atlantic patience.  
We too have cargo, dear; not gold, but maps  
of rooms we left, of children’s voices thinning,  
of summers folded small as railway tickets.  
The Loire runs west regardless, royal, shallow,  
braiding its sandbanks under poplars’ smoke.

So mark the route. Chinon for noon; Saumur  
if legs allow; then Angers, perhaps, or nothing—  
the blessed blank beyond the printed edge.  
Spring’s in the glass. The roads uncurl like vines.  
High time: not late, not yet; the hour made high  
by being nearly gone, and therefore shining.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem that sounds like Geoffrey Hill or a Hill pastiche: morally charged diction breaking down into playful fragments, historical references, French geography, “Tomorrow and tomorrow,” and a repeated refrain of “High time.”
counterfactuals.output:
**High time**

High time. The chancery clock coughs up its brass  
and calls it mercy; writs in a damp hand  
unseal the century—Agincourt, Sedan,  
Verdun’s black rosary of mud and gas.  

Tomorrow and tomorrow: the footfalls  
of clerks through corridors of cancelled grace.  
A king’s face flakes from the coin; the coin falls  
into the Rhône, or Loir, or some such place.  

High time. At Chartres the blue keeps its oath,  
though we do not. Rouen smokes in the rain.  
Bayeux unrolls its beasts, its stitched betroth—  
O Harold, eye-full, oath-sick, slain again.  

*Droit? droite?* The tongue trips; the map grows witty:  
Béziers, Bourges, Blois—bright beads, blots, blows.  
Who profits by the ash of a good city?  
Ask the archive. Ask the rose.  

High time. The saints have pawned their haloes;  
the magistrates rehearse a tender fraud.  
*Pardon, monsieur*—the scaffold has its gallows-  
humour, its little jig before the Lord.  

Tomorrow and tomorrow. Macbeth’s ember  
sits in the grate of Europe, barely red.  
We warm our hands at what we misremember:  
the treaty signed, the hostage fed, the dead.  

High time: for penance? No—pennants, pennons,  
pennies on eyelids, puns in the nave.  
The bells of Nantes make nonsense canons:  
save what you can; what you can’t, engrave.  

High time. And still the conscience, stony,  
chips at its Latin: *mea maxima culpa*.  
History, that grandee, bows too slowly;  
the child in the dust says: hoopla, hoopla.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental lyric monologue starting from the phrase “Spring pricks a little. I get out the maps,” including the quoted line “stooped to truth and moralized his song,” and ending tenderly with “High time, my love. High time and a long time yet.”
counterfactuals.output:
Spring pricks a little. I get out the maps,  
not to go, not yet, but to touch the blue veins  
of rivers with one finger and remember  
how distance once behaved like mercy.

The window is doing its green arithmetic.  
One bud, then five. One bird, then everywhere.  
I have been indoors with my weather,  
folding and refolding the same wrong letter,  
asking the kettle for counsel,  
asking the floorboards what they know of return.

There are countries named for hunger,  
countries named for saints, countries named  
after men who never knelt except to claim them.  
I circle none of these. I draw instead  
a small, warm province around your chair.

Last night I dreamed a poet “stooped to truth and moralized his song,”  
and woke ashamed of all my cleverness.  
What is the use of silvering grief  
when grief only wants a cup of water?  
What is the use of singing beautifully  
if the beloved has left the room  
to stand alone among the dishes?

Listen—spring is at the latch again,  
with its rude little thorns, its light like a child  
who will not apologize for being born.  
The garden begins its argument from scratch.  
Mud makes a dark vow.  
The worms, blind archivists, revise the earth.

And I, who have mistaken motion for arrival,  
lay the maps across the table  
like old bandages. Here is the road  
we did not take because the rain had softened it.  
Here is the town where we bought peaches  
and ate them over the sink, laughing  
at the sweetness running down our wrists.  
Here is the border no one saw us cross.  
Here is the sea, still practicing infinity.

Come here. No prophecy now.  
No grand republic of the healed.  
Only your hand, older than my fear,  
finding mine among the paper mountains.  
Only the lamp consenting to the evening.  
Only the dog turning once in sleep  
before trusting the world again.

The clocks clear their throats.  
The lilacs loosen.  
Every road remembers being dust.

High time, my love. High time and a long time yet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a fragmented travel-and-aging love poem set around the Brenne valley, Montoire, and Château-Renault, using archaic diction, self-corrections, literary echoes, and the motif of taking off glasses to read a map.
counterfactuals.output:
**Brenne, with Spectacles Removed**

At Montoire—nay, a little after—  
where the Brenne goes under its willows  
like a grey thought under green hair,  
thou didst take off thy glasses  
to read the map.

So near the paper, love, thy face  
became a country also:  
crease-road, river-vein, the small red towns  
of age kindled at the cheek.

“Here,” thou saidst—  
no, not saidst; breathed—  
“the valley turns.”

And I, poor pilgrim,  
who had followed other turnings—  
Dante’s dark wood,  
Du Bellay’s little Loire lament,  
old Ronsard’s rose already shedding—  
looked where thy finger, tremulous and kingly,  
made a bridge of itself.

Brenne, Brenne—  
brown syllable, water worn,  
carrying mills, Sundays, swallows,  
our late hour.

At Château-Renault the roofs were slate,  
or memory makes them so;  
the road climbed, then repented,  
then climbed again.  
We bought pears. We quarrelled softly.  
We forgot why.  
This too is love:  
to lose the cause, keep the hand.

O thou, my fair, my faded—  
forgive: my fairer for fading—  
when thou removest thy spectacles  
the world grows blurred to me,  
yet the map is plain to thee.

What art thou reading there?  
Not Tours, nor Blois, nor Vendôme—  
but some white margin past the fold,  
where inns have no names,  
where the beloved arrive  
unannounced, unburdened,  
without luggage, without years.

Stay.  
Nay—go slowly.

Fold not the map yet.

Let Brenne valley lie open  
between us on the table,  
its blue thread thin as a wrist-pulse,  
and let Montoire’s bells, far off,  
spell what they have always spelt  
to travellers and the old:

Return, return—  
though none returneth whole.

And if, at dusk, thou canst not see  
the road for mist,  
take off thy glasses once again,  
bend close, my dear,  
my dear old guide,  
and read us home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
